(CNN) -- More than 100 countries attending a conference in Dublin, Ireland formally adopted a treaty Friday to ban cluster bombs -- a large, unreliable and inaccurate weapon that often affects civilians long after the end of armed conflict. Cluster bombs are usually air-dropped shells that eject multiple small bomblets to kill enemy soldiers. A document released by Ireland's Department of Foreign Affairs says the countries agreed never to use cluster munitions or the explosive bomblets they contain. The countries also agreed never to develop, acquire, retain or transfer cluster munitions. Countries attending the 11-day conference agreed to the treaty Wednesday but formally signed it Friday. The accord calls for a total, immediate ban of the weapons, strong standards to protect those injured by them, contaminated areas to be cleaned up as quickly as possible and for the weapons to be immediately destroyed, he said. Thomas Nash, coordinator of the CMC campaigning organization, said Wednesday: "This is a great achievement for everyone who has been working hard to see the end of 40 years of suffering from these weapons." Though some of the biggest makers of cluster bombs, including the United States, Russia, China and Israel, were not involved in the talks and have not signed the accord, organizers predicted that those nations would nevertheless be pressured into compliance. "Take the United States," Nash said. "Almost all of its allies are here. They've decided to ban these weapons. That's going to make it extremely difficult, if not impossible, for the United States to ever use these weapons again, either on its own or in joint operations." The agreement requires the destruction of stockpiles of the weapons within eight years, he said. Cluster munitions, which break apart in flight to scatter hundreds of smaller bomblets, are what the International Committee of the Red Cross calls a "persistent humanitarian problem." Most of a cluster bomb's bomblets are meant to explode on impact, but many do not. Estimates show the weapons fail to explode on impact between 10 and 40 percent of the time, the Red Cross says. That means unexploded bomblets lie scattered across a target area, often exploding only when handled or disturbed -- posing a serious risk to civilians. Last week, Acting Assistant Secretary for Political-Military Affairs Stephen D. Mull called it "an absolute moral obligation" to rid a battlefield of unexploded ordnance after the battle. But he also predicted that the United States would not agree to any ban. "We think that it is going to be impossible to ban cluster munitions... because these are weapons that have a certain military utility and are of use," Mull said. "The United States relies on them as an important part of our own defense strategy." Instead, he urged that the weapons be regulated "to take humanitarian considerations into account" and that "technological fixes" be pursued that would render them harmless after a battle. During the 34-day war in Lebanon in 2006, the United Nations estimated that Israel dropped 4 million bomblets, 1 million of which may not have exploded, according to the International Committee of the Red Cross. More than 250 civilians and bomb-disposal operators have been killed or injured by them in southern Lebanon since the war ended. Cluster bombs were also used in the 1999 war in Kosovo. Lt. Col. Jim Burke, a military adviser to the Irish Defense Forces said they quickly became a major killer of civilians. In more than 20 countries, according to the ICRC, cluster bombs have created lasting "no-go" areas, rendering them as dangerous as minefields. Laos is the most affected country. Millions of bomblets dropped during the Vietnam War continue to kill civilians more than three decades later. Still, militaries consider cluster bombs important for use against multiple targets dispersed over a wide area, such as tanks or military personnel moving across the landscape. A single bomb containing hundreds of submunitions can cover more than 18 square miles. CNN's Jacqueline Clyne contributed to this report.

Cluster bombs are typically air-dropped shells that release multiple small bomblets designed to kill enemy soldiers. According to a document released by Ireland’s Department of Foreign Affairs, the participating countries agreed never to use cluster munitions or the explosive bomblets they contain. They also pledged never to develop, acquire, retain, or transfer cluster munitions.

The countries attending the 11-day conference reached agreement on the treaty Wednesday and formally signed it Friday. The accord calls for a total and immediate ban on the weapons, strong protections for those injured by them, the rapid cleanup of contaminated areas, and the immediate destruction of the weapons, according to Thomas Nash, coordinator of the CMC campaigning organization.

“This is a great achievement for everyone who has been working hard to see the end of 40 years of suffering from these weapons,” Nash said Wednesday.

Although several of the largest manufacturers of cluster bombs—including the United States, Russia, China, and Israel—did not participate in the talks and have not signed the accord, organizers predicted that those nations would nevertheless face pressure to comply.

“Take the United States,” Nash said. “Almost all of its allies are here. They’ve decided to ban these weapons. That’s going to make it extremely difficult, if not impossible, for the United States to ever use these weapons again, either on its own or in joint operations.”

The agreement requires participating countries to destroy their stockpiles of the weapons within eight years, Nash said.

Cluster munitions, which break apart in flight and scatter hundreds of smaller bomblets, constitute what the International Committee of the Red Cross calls a “persistent humanitarian problem.”

Most of a cluster bomb’s bomblets are intended to explode on impact, but many fail to do so. According to Red Cross estimates, between 10 and 40 percent do not detonate on impact. As a result, unexploded bomblets remain scattered across target areas, often exploding only when handled or disturbed and posing a serious risk to civilians.

Last week, Acting Assistant Secretary for Political-Military Affairs Stephen D. Mull called it “an absolute moral obligation” to clear a battlefield of unexploded ordnance after fighting has ended. However, he also predicted that the United States would not agree to a ban.

“We think that it is going to be impossible to ban cluster munitions ... because these are weapons that have a certain military utility and are of use,” Mull said. “The United States relies on them as an important part of our own defense strategy.”

Instead, he urged that the weapons be regulated “to take humanitarian considerations into account” and that “technological fixes” be pursued to render them harmless after a battle.

During the 34-day war in Lebanon in 2006, the United Nations estimated that Israel dropped 4 million bomblets, 1 million of which may not have exploded, according to the International Committee of the Red Cross. Since the war ended, more than 250 civilians and bomb-disposal operators in southern Lebanon have been killed or injured by the bomblets.

Cluster bombs were also used during the 1999 war in Kosovo. Lt. Col. Jim Burke, a military adviser to the Irish Defense Forces, said they quickly became a major cause of civilian deaths.

According to the ICRC, cluster bombs have created enduring “no-go” areas in more than 20 countries, making them as dangerous as minefields. Laos is the country most severely affected. Millions of bomblets dropped during the Vietnam War continue to kill civilians more than three decades later.

Nevertheless, military forces consider cluster bombs important for use against multiple targets dispersed over a wide area, such as tanks or military personnel moving across the landscape. A single bomb containing hundreds of submunitions can cover more than 18 square miles.

DUBLIN, Ireland (CNN) — Delegates from more than 100 nations formally approved an international treaty Friday prohibiting cluster bombs, weapons widely criticized for their size, poor reliability and lack of precision, as well as for the danger they pose to civilians long after fighting has stopped.

Cluster bombs are generally delivered from aircraft and release numerous smaller explosive devices designed to kill enemy troops. According to a document issued by Ireland’s Department of Foreign Affairs, participating countries pledged never to use cluster munitions or their bomblets. They also committed not to manufacture, obtain, stockpile or transfer the weapons.

The nations at the 11-day Dublin conference reached agreement on the treaty Wednesday and formally adopted it Friday. The pact imposes a complete and immediate prohibition, establishes strong protections for victims, requires contaminated land to be cleared as rapidly as possible and calls for the prompt destruction of the weapons. Existing stockpiles must be eliminated within eight years.

Thomas Nash, coordinator of the Cluster Munition Coalition, or CMC, welcomed the agreement Wednesday, calling it a major accomplishment for those who had spent years trying to end four decades of suffering caused by the weapons.

Several leading producers of cluster bombs—including the United States, Russia, China and Israel—did not participate in the negotiations and have not joined the agreement. Organizers nevertheless said the treaty would create pressure for those governments to follow its standards.

Nash pointed to the United States as an example, noting that nearly all of its allies attended the conference and chose to outlaw the weapons. Their decision, he said, would make future U.S. use of cluster bombs—whether independently or in joint military missions—extremely difficult, and perhaps impossible.

Cluster munitions separate while airborne, spreading hundreds of smaller bomblets across the ground. The International Committee of the Red Cross describes them as a continuing humanitarian threat. Although the bomblets are intended to detonate when they strike, many fail to do so. The Red Cross estimates that between 10% and 40% remain unexploded.

These unexploded devices can stay scattered throughout the targeted area and may detonate only after being touched or disturbed, creating a severe and prolonged hazard for civilians.

The previous week, Stephen D. Mull, then acting U.S. assistant secretary for political-military affairs, said there was “an absolute moral obligation” to clear unexploded ammunition from a battlefield once combat had ended. However, he also said the United States was unlikely to accept a ban because cluster munitions had military value and formed an important element of the country’s defense strategy.

Rather than outlawing them, Mull advocated rules that would address humanitarian concerns. He also called for technological solutions capable of making the weapons harmless after hostilities were over.

During the 34-day Lebanon war in 2006, the United Nations estimated that Israel released 4 million bomblets. According to the International Committee of the Red Cross, as many as 1 million may have failed to explode. Since the conflict ended, those devices have killed or wounded more than 250 civilians and bomb-disposal personnel in southern Lebanon.

Cluster bombs were also deployed during the 1999 Kosovo war. Lt. Col. Jim Burke, a military adviser to the Irish Defense Forces, said they soon became a significant cause of civilian deaths.

The ICRC reports that cluster munitions have left enduring exclusion zones in more than 20 countries, making those areas as hazardous as minefields. Laos has suffered the greatest impact. Millions of bomblets dropped there during the Vietnam War were still killing civilians more than 30 years later.

Despite those humanitarian consequences, armed forces regard cluster bombs as useful against numerous targets spread across a broad area, including tanks and military personnel moving over open terrain. One weapon carrying hundreds of submunitions can affect an area larger than 18 square miles.

CNN’s Jacqueline Clyne contributed to the report.

The agreement bans their use, production, development, acquisition, stockpiling, retention and transfer, and requires participating states to destroy existing stockpiles within eight years.

The treaty also obliges governments to clear areas contaminated by unexploded bomblets, generally within 10 years, and to provide medical care, rehabilitation, psychological support and social and economic assistance to victims and affected communities. It establishes mechanisms for international cooperation and allows deadlines to be extended in exceptional circumstances.

Cluster munitions have been used in conflicts for decades. Because they disperse explosives across broad areas, they can kill civilians during attacks without adequately distinguishing between military and civilian targets. In addition, many bomblets fail to detonate on impact and remain dangerous for years, effectively becoming small land mines that threaten farmers, children and others long after fighting has ended. Unexploded submunitions have caused extensive casualties in countries including Laos, Lebanon, Afghanistan and Iraq.

Supporters described the Dublin accord as a major humanitarian achievement comparable to the 1997 treaty banning antipersonnel land mines. The negotiations were driven by governments, humanitarian organizations and survivors frustrated by the slow pace of talks within traditional arms-control forums.

They maintain that cluster munitions can have legitimate military uses and argue that newer models are more reliable. Nevertheless, campaigners said the participation of many of those countries’ allies could stigmatize the weapons, complicate their deployment in joint operations and create political pressure on nonsignatories to change their policies.

The convention was scheduled to open for signature in Oslo later in 2008 and to enter into force after the required number of countries ratified it. **More than 100 nations adopt cluster bomb treaty in Dublin**

**DUBLIN, Ireland** — More than 100 countries adopted a landmark treaty Friday banning cluster munitions, weapons that humanitarian groups say kill civilians during conflicts and can remain deadly for years after fighting ends.

The agreement, approved at an international conference in Dublin, prohibits the use, production, transfer and stockpiling of cluster bombs. It also requires participating nations to destroy their stockpiles, clear contaminated areas and assist victims.

Cluster munitions scatter dozens or hundreds of smaller explosives, known as bomblets, across a wide area. Many fail to detonate on impact, leaving behind hazards that can later kill or maim civilians, including children.

The United States did not participate in the negotiations and opposes the ban, arguing that cluster munitions have legitimate military uses and that eliminating them could endanger troops and coalition operations. Other major producers or users, including Russia and China, also stayed outside the process.

Supporters hailed the agreement as a major humanitarian breakthrough, comparing it to the international treaty banning anti-personnel land mines. Campaigners cited civilian casualties from cluster munitions used in conflicts including Lebanon, Iraq, Afghanistan and Southeast Asia.

The treaty includes limited provisions allowing military cooperation between signatory nations and countries that have not joined — a key concern for U.S. allies. It is expected to be formally opened for signature in Oslo later in the year and will take effect after the required number of countries ratify it.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain the 2008 international agreement to prohibit cluster munitions, why these weapons pose a lasting danger to civilians, and which major countries declined to participate.
counterfactuals.output:
The **2008 Convention on Cluster Munitions (CCM)** is an international treaty adopted in Dublin in May 2008 and opened for signature in Oslo that December. It entered into force in 2010.

The convention prohibits participating states from:

- Using cluster munitions  
- Developing, producing, acquiring, stockpiling, or transferring them  
- Assisting or encouraging anyone to carry out those activities  

It also requires states to destroy stockpiles, clear contaminated land, educate populations about the risks, and assist victims.

### Why cluster munitions remain dangerous

Cluster munitions disperse dozens or hundreds of smaller “bomblets” over a wide area. This creates two major civilian hazards:

1. **Wide-area effects:** They cannot reliably distinguish soldiers from civilians when used in or near populated areas.
2. **Unexploded submunitions:** A significant number of bomblets may fail to detonate on impact. They can remain lethal for years or decades, functioning much like landmines. Farmers, displaced people returning home, and children—sometimes attracted by their small or colorful appearance—are especially vulnerable.

Unexploded bomblets also make farmland, roads, and buildings unsafe, delaying reconstruction and economic recovery after a conflict.

### Major countries that did not join

Several major military powers and cluster-munition producers or stockpilers declined to sign the convention, including:

- **United States**
- **Russia**
- **China**
- **India**
- **Pakistan**
- **Israel**
- **South Korea**

Other non-participants include **Ukraine** and several states in the Middle East and Asia. These governments have generally argued that cluster munitions retain military utility and that their risks can be reduced through technical improvements or operational restrictions. Because key powers remain outside the treaty, the prohibition is legally binding only on states that have joined, although the convention has helped create a broader international stigma against the weapons.

counterfactuals.output:
# Cluster-Munitions Treaty Sets Global Ban, but Unexploded Bomblets Still Kill Decades Later

**GENEVA —** The Convention on Cluster Munitions has established one of the world’s most comprehensive prohibitions on a class of conventional weapons, requiring member states not only to stop using cluster bombs but also to destroy stockpiles, clear contaminated land and assist survivors.

Adopted in Dublin in May 2008, opened for signature in Oslo that December and in force since August 2010, the treaty emerged from mounting evidence that cluster munitions cause extensive civilian harm during attacks and leave behind large numbers of explosive remnants that can remain lethal for generations.

More than 100 countries have joined the convention. However, several major military powers and producers—including the United States, Russia, China, India, Pakistan and Israel—remain outside it.

## What the convention requires

The treaty prohibits states parties from using, developing, producing, acquiring, stockpiling, retaining or transferring cluster munitions. It also bars them from assisting, encouraging or inducing anyone to engage in those activities.

Cluster munitions are weapons that open in the air and scatter dozens or hundreds of smaller explosives, commonly called submunitions or bomblets, over a wide area. They can be delivered by aircraft, missiles, rockets or artillery.

The convention generally requires participating countries to:

- **Destroy stockpiles within eight years** of becoming legally bound by the treaty.
- **Clear cluster-munition-contaminated areas within 10 years**, unless an extension is approved.
- **Identify and mark hazardous areas**, warn local populations and provide risk education.
- **Assist victims**, including through medical care, rehabilitation, psychological support and social and economic inclusion.
- **Report on stockpiles, destruction and clearance**, allowing international monitoring of implementation.
- **Cooperate internationally**, including by providing technical and financial assistance to affected countries.

The convention permits states to retain a limited number of munitions and submunitions for training in detection, clearance and destruction techniques. It also contains provisions addressing military cooperation with countries that are not party to the treaty, an issue that generated debate during negotiations.

Certain weapons containing submunitions are excluded from the definition if they meet technical safeguards intended to reduce indiscriminate effects and the risk of unexploded ordnance—for example, if they carry a small number of individually targetable submunitions equipped with electronic self-destruct and self-deactivation mechanisms.

## Campaigners hail the ban but warn of loopholes

The Cluster Munition Coalition, a global civil-society network that led the campaign for the treaty, has described the convention as a major humanitarian and disarmament achievement. Human Rights Watch, the International Committee of the Red Cross and other organizations have similarly argued that the treaty created a strong international norm against weapons whose effects are difficult to confine to military targets.

Campaigners point to the destruction of millions of stockpiled submunitions, national bans and sustained clearance programs as evidence that the convention has changed state behavior even beyond its formal membership.

But advocates have also criticized countries that refuse to join and warned that continued use by nonparties undermines the treaty’s humanitarian goals. They have urged member states to condemn any use of cluster munitions, including by allies, and to interpret the ban on assistance strictly.

Another concern is funding. Clearing bomblets is slow and dangerous, while survivors often require lifelong medical treatment and economic support. Campaigners say affected states—many of them developing countries—cannot meet their obligations without sustained international assistance.

## A weapon with a persistent failure problem

Cluster weapons pose two distinct dangers. During an attack, their wide-area footprint can place civilians at risk, particularly when the munitions are used in or near populated areas. Afterward, bomblets that fail to detonate can function much like land mines.

Manufacturers and armed forces have sometimes cited failure rates in the low single digits under controlled test conditions. Field evidence, however, has frequently shown much higher rates—often 10% or more and, in some circumstances, 30% to 40%.

Failure rates depend on several factors, including the age and design of the weapon, storage conditions, release altitude, vegetation, soft ground and whether bomblets strike at the angle needed to activate their fuzes.

Even a low failure rate can leave a large hazard. A weapon dispersing 200 bomblets with a 5% failure rate may scatter roughly 10 unexploded devices. When hundreds or thousands of cluster munitions are used, the resulting contamination can extend across farms, roads, homes and schools.

The small size and sometimes bright coloring of submunitions can make them especially dangerous to children. Farmers, scrap-metal collectors, construction workers and returning displaced families are also at high risk.

## Lebanon: Up to one million unexploded submunitions

The consequences were stark after the 2006 war between Israel and Hezbollah in Lebanon.

United Nations estimates indicated that Israel fired cluster munitions containing approximately **four million submunitions** into southern Lebanon. The United Nations said as many as **one million bomblets may initially have failed to explode**.

UN officials also reported that an estimated 90% of the cluster strikes occurred during the final 72 hours of the conflict, when a ceasefire was approaching. Israel disputed some criticism of its conduct and said its weapons had been used against military targets in accordance with international law, while rights groups argued that the scale and location of the attacks created an unacceptable civilian hazard.

After residents returned home, unexploded bomblets were found in houses, gardens, fields and along roads. They killed and injured civilians and clearance personnel and disrupted agriculture in a region heavily dependent on tobacco, olive and fruit production.

Extensive clearance has removed large numbers of submunitions, but the Lebanon experience became one of the principal catalysts for negotiations that produced the 2008 convention.

## Kosovo: Postwar casualties after NATO strikes

During NATO’s 1999 air campaign against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, alliance forces dropped approximately **1,392 cluster bombs containing about 289,000 submunitions** over Kosovo, according to NATO figures frequently cited by humanitarian organizations.

Unexploded bomblets continued to cause casualties after the conflict. Children were among those killed or wounded after encountering the small devices, some of which lay on the surface rather than being buried like conventional mines.

The danger complicated the return of refugees and displaced people. It also exposed a technical problem for clearance teams: local populations often treated contaminated areas as minefields, but cluster submunitions could be more widely scattered and less systematically laid than land mines.

NATO later acknowledged that cluster munitions had caused civilian casualties during the campaign. The Kosovo experience strengthened calls for more accurate data on strike locations and for belligerents to provide clearance organizations with detailed records immediately after hostilities.

## Laos: A legacy measured in generations

No country illustrates the long-term consequences more dramatically than Laos.

From 1964 to 1973, during the Indochina war, the United States dropped more than **two million tons of ordnance** on Laos. That included an estimated **270 million cluster submunitions**.

Commonly cited estimates suggest that up to **80 million bomblets failed to explode**, although the precise number is impossible to verify. Decades later, unexploded ordnance continues to kill and injure people and restrict access to agricultural land.

The contamination is particularly severe in rural areas, where families depend on farming and where metal from wartime ordnance may be collected and sold. Development projects—including road building, schools, irrigation and electricity lines—often require costly surveys and clearance before work can begin.

Laos became a leading voice in the campaign against cluster munitions and hosted the convention’s first meeting of states parties in Vientiane in 2010. Its experience helped shape the treaty’s emphasis on clearance, risk education and victim assistance, not merely a ban on future use.

## A strong norm without universal membership

Supporters say the Convention on Cluster Munitions has stigmatized the weapon, reduced production and trade, and prompted states to destroy enormous stockpiles. No state party may legally use cluster munitions, and members are expected to press countries outside the convention to abandon them.

Yet the treaty’s impact is limited by the absence of major users and stockpilers. Cluster munitions have continued to appear in armed conflicts, demonstrating that the global norm remains incomplete.

For affected communities, the measure of success is not only how many governments sign the convention, but how quickly contaminated land is made safe and survivors receive support.

The examples of Lebanon, Kosovo and Laos show why campaigners pursued a categorical ban: a cluster strike may last only seconds, but its unexploded bomblets can shape civilian life for years—or, in the case of Laos, for generations.

counterfactuals.output:
At the 11-day Dublin Diplomatic Conference in May 2008, delegates from more than 100 countries agreed by consensus on the **Convention on Cluster Munitions**. The treaty prohibited the use, production, transfer, and stockpiling of most cluster bombs, required existing stockpiles to be destroyed—generally within eight years—and contaminated areas to be cleared, while also requiring assistance for victims. It was formally opened for signature in Oslo later that year.

The United States did not join the Dublin process or support the treaty. Washington argued that cluster munitions still had important military uses, particularly against dispersed or moving targets, and that an immediate categorical ban could endanger U.S. forces and allies that relied on U.S. capabilities. # Cluster munitions: Why much of the world has banned them — and why some militaries still want them

**CNN —** Cluster munitions can scatter dozens or even hundreds of smaller explosives across an area in a matter of seconds. Supporters say that makes them effective against dispersed troops, vehicles and air defenses. Critics say the same feature makes them inherently dangerous to civilians — both during an attack and for years afterward.

The 2008 **Convention on Cluster Munitions**, which entered into force in 2010, prohibits participating countries from using, producing, acquiring, stockpiling or transferring the weapons. It also requires the destruction of stockpiles, clearance of contaminated land and assistance for victims.

More than 100 countries have joined the treaty. But several major military powers — including the United States, Russia and China — remain outside it. Ukraine is also not a party.

## How cluster bombs work

A cluster munition is typically a bomb, missile or artillery projectile that opens in the air and releases multiple smaller explosives, often called submunitions or bomblets.

Those bomblets spread over a wide “footprint,” allowing one weapon to strike multiple targets. Depending on their design, they may be intended to destroy armored vehicles, penetrate structures, start fires or injure personnel.

The danger does not end when the attack is over. Some bomblets fail to explode as designed because of manufacturing defects, soft ground, vegetation or other conditions. The unexploded submunitions can remain lethal, functioning much like land mines if disturbed.

Failure rates vary widely by model, age and battlefield conditions. Humanitarian groups have repeatedly argued that real-world dud rates can be significantly higher than manufacturers’ estimates.

## A threat long after war ends

Unexploded cluster bomblets have killed and injured civilians decades after conflicts. Farmers can encounter them while working fields, children may mistake them for toys, and families returning home may find them in roads, gardens and damaged buildings.

Laos remains one of the starkest examples. The country was heavily bombed during the Vietnam War era, and unexploded submunitions continue to contaminate large areas. Cluster-munition remnants have also caused casualties in countries including Lebanon, Iraq, Afghanistan and parts of the former Yugoslavia.

Beyond deaths and injuries, contamination can prevent people from farming, rebuilding homes or using roads and schools. Clearance is slow, dangerous and expensive because individual bomblets may be scattered across broad areas and hidden by soil or vegetation.

The treaty’s supporters say those consequences are central to the case for a ban. They argue that cluster munitions cannot reliably distinguish between military targets and civilians when used near populated areas, and that unexploded bomblets create an unacceptable postwar hazard.

## Why some militaries retain them

Countries that have not joined the convention generally argue that cluster munitions still have legitimate military uses.

A single cluster weapon can attack a wide area containing dispersed forces, armored formations, artillery positions or air-defense systems. Military planners say that, in some circumstances, replacing that capability with conventional “unitary” warheads would require many more missiles, shells or aircraft sorties.

Supporters also contend that newer cluster munitions can be designed with electronic fuzes, self-destruct mechanisms or self-deactivation features intended to reduce the number of unexploded bomblets. They say weapons with low tested failure rates should be distinguished from older, less reliable models.

Another argument is deterrence: Some governments are reluctant to abandon the weapons while potential adversaries retain large stockpiles. They also note that international humanitarian law already requires armed forces to distinguish between civilian and military targets, avoid indiscriminate attacks and limit disproportionate harm.

Critics respond that technical safeguards can fail and that even fully functioning bomblets can cause widespread civilian casualties if dispersed over populated areas. They say the weapon’s broad-area effects and enduring contamination make meaningful risk reduction difficult.

The debate therefore centers on a fundamental trade-off: the battlefield efficiency cluster munitions may offer against dispersed targets, weighed against their potential to kill civilians indiscriminately and leave a deadly legacy long after the fighting stops.
